n: The title calls this “the song of songs” — the greatest or most beautiful song. It is a collection of love poetry between a bride and her bridegroom, connected with Solomon. In his Bible revision, Joseph Smith noted that he did not regard this book as inspired scripture.

f.g: A Hebrew superlative, like “holy of holies” — the finest song.
JST manuscript note: “The Songs of Solomon are not inspired writings.”

n: The bride speaks first, longing for her beloved’s affection. She says his love is more delightful than wine, the drink of celebration.

f.g: Wine symbolized joy and festivity in ancient Israel.

n: His fragrance is lovely, and his very name — his character and reputation — is like perfume poured out. No wonder the young women admire him.

f.g: Fragrance.
Young women; maidens.

n: She asks him to draw her close. She has been brought into the king’s rooms, and her friends join in rejoicing at their love.

f.g: Take me with you; pull me near.
Or “rightly do they love you.”

n: She tells the women of Jerusalem that though her skin is dark from the sun, she is lovely — like the black goat-hair tents of Kedar or the fine curtains of Solomon.

f.g: An Arabian desert tribe descended from Ishmael, known for black tents (Genesis 25:13).
Lovely, attractive.

n: She explains her sun-darkened skin: her angry brothers made her work outdoors in the vineyards, so she couldn’t care for her own “vineyard” — her own appearance.

f.g: Her brothers.
Probably herself — her beauty and person.

n: She asks her beloved, pictured as a shepherd, where he rests his flock at noon, so she doesn’t have to wander among other shepherds looking for him.

f.g: Or “one who is veiled” — wandering about like a stranger.

n: The answer (perhaps from him or from her friends): follow the tracks of the flock and graze your young goats near the shepherds’ tents, and you’ll find him.

f.g: Young goats.

n: Now the bridegroom speaks. He compares her to a splendid mare among Pharaoh’s chariot horses — a compliment to her beauty and grace that stood out.
Her face is beautiful framed by strings of jewelry, and her neck by golden necklaces.

f.g: Strings of beads or ornaments.

n: He (or the friends) promises to make her even finer ornaments of gold and silver.

f.g: Small ornaments or beads.

n: The bride says that while the king reclines at his table, her perfume spreads its fragrance — a way of saying her love reaches out to him.

f.g: Nard, a costly fragrant oil from the Himalayas (compare Mark 14:3).

n: She describes her beloved as a little pouch of myrrh worn close to her heart — precious and always near.

f.g: A fragrant resin often worn in a small bag around the neck.
Between.

n: He is to her like a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi, a lush oasis beside the Dead Sea.

f.g: Henna, a shrub with fragrant blossoms.
A spring-fed oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea (1 Samuel 24:1).

n: The groom praises her beauty twice for emphasis. Her eyes are like doves — gentle, soft, and faithful.

f.g: A picture of gentleness, innocence, and constancy.

n: She answers that he is handsome and delightful. Their resting place is like green grass, a picture of a fresh, peaceful setting.
Their “house” is like a forest of cedar and fir — whether a real garden setting or a poetic home, it is beautiful and strong.

f.g: Prized, fragrant wood from Lebanon, used in Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:9).
